subject: Society and Culture
name: Society and Culture, Year 12
about: HSC, Continuity and change, the PIP and depth studies
syllabus: NSW Society and Culture Stage 6 Syllabus (2013), HSC (Year 12) course, the core and the four depth studies

units.title: Social and cultural continuity and change

points.title: The nature of continuity and change
points.brief: Societies change in some ways while keeping others, and studying a country over time shows how tradition and change shape each other.

points.title: Agents of change
points.brief: People, groups, new technologies, the economy and events such as wars can all bring social change.

points.title: Modernisation and westernisation
points.brief: Modernisation is the change from traditional to industrial and urban life. Westernisation is taking on the ways of Western countries. They are not the same.

points.title: Resistance to change
points.brief: People resist change to protect tradition, identity, power or security, and resistance can slow or reshape it.

points.title: Theories of change
points.brief: Functionalism sees change as a society adjusting to stay stable. Conflict theory sees it as the result of struggles between groups for power.

points.title: Choosing a topic
points.brief: A good PIP topic is something the student cares about, is narrow enough to research well and links to the course concepts.

points.title: The cross-cultural component
points.brief: The PIP must compare the topic across cultures, groups or times, showing how experiences differ.

points.title: Choosing a mix of methods
points.brief: Using more than one research method, such as a questionnaire and interviews, gives stronger, more balanced findings.

points.title: Writing up the project
points.brief: The PIP has an introduction, a log of the research process, a central material discussing findings and a conclusion, with a resource list.

points.title: Personal reflection in the PIP
points.brief: The project shows the student's own thinking and what they learned, while keeping the research objective.

points.title: What popular culture is
points.brief: Popular culture is the music, film, games, sport, fashion and media enjoyed by large numbers of people, often spread through mass media.

points.title: Popular culture and identity
points.brief: People use popular culture to express who they are and to belong to groups, such as fans of a band or a sport.

points.title: Commodification
points.brief: Turning culture into products to be bought and sold, such as merchandise and streaming subscriptions.

points.title: Global popular culture
points.brief: Media companies and the internet spread popular culture worldwide, which can mix cultures or crowd out local ones.

points.title: Power in popular culture
points.brief: A few large companies control much of what is produced and promoted, while social media lets ordinary people create and spread culture too.

points.title: What belief systems and ideologies are
points.brief: A belief system is a set of ideas about meaning and how to live, such as a religion. An ideology is a set of political or social ideas, such as liberalism.

points.title: Belief systems and identity
points.brief: Belief systems give people a sense of identity, community and guidance on how to act.

points.title: Belief systems and power
points.brief: Belief systems and ideologies can support those in power or be used to challenge them.

points.title: Continuity and change in beliefs
points.brief: Beliefs change through contact with other ideas, new technology and social change, while many traditions stay strong.

points.title: Secularisation
points.brief: The decline of religion's influence on public life, which is uneven across countries and groups.

points.title: What inclusion and exclusion mean
points.brief: Social inclusion is being able to take part fully in society. Exclusion is being shut out of work, services, decisions or social life.

points.title: Causes of exclusion
points.brief: Poverty, disability, discrimination, location, age and lack of education can all exclude people.

points.title: Effects of exclusion
points.brief: Exclusion can harm health, wellbeing, income and a sense of belonging, and can carry on across generations.

points.title: Strategies for inclusion
points.brief: Laws against discrimination, accessible services, education and community programs help include people.

points.title: Inclusion and power
points.brief: Groups with more power often set the rules of who is included, and excluded groups may work to change them.

points.title: Conformity
points.brief: Conformity is following the norms and expectations of a group, often because of social pressure or a wish to belong.

points.title: Nonconformity
points.brief: Nonconformity is going against the norms, which can be a personal choice, a protest or a way to form a new group.

points.title: Sanctions
points.brief: Groups reward conformity and punish nonconformity, through formal sanctions such as laws and informal ones such as disapproval.

points.title: Subcultures
points.brief: A subculture is a group with values and styles different from the wider society, such as skaters or gamers.

points.title: Theories of conformity
points.brief: Studies such as Asch's experiments show how strongly group pressure can push people to agree, even when the group is wrong.
